newsitem.title: USA: States press administration to take nuclear waste.
newsitem.headline: States press administration to take nuclear waste.

text.p: States are stepping up pressure on the Clinton administration to take over nuclear waste from power plants next year, a National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners spokesman said Monday.

NARUC last Friday joined a lawsuit filed by 46 state agencies asking the court to let utilities stop paying $600 million a year into a U.S. nuclear waste fund and make the government take away their spent fuel, as required under law.
The main concern for state regulators, who set local electricity rates, is that utility customers who paid the nuclear waste fee for the last 13 years are being cheated.
When regulators approved the building of nuclear power plants "customers told these state commissioners we don't want the waste stored here," said NARUC spokesman John Gawronski.

Money from the nuclear waste fund is being used to investigate Yucca Mountain in Nevada as a permanent dump, which was supposed to have been ready in 1998. The Energy Department does not expect a dump to be ready until 2010.

The Clinton administration has refused to back bills to build an interim facility next to Yucca Mountain while the site is still being tested. But states do not want to be saddled with the waste in the interim.
"Because utilities have planned according to the current law, in the interim we need to relieve those utilities ... until the repository is in place," Gawronski said.
Without a place to store the fuel, industry sources have said the government's only way out would be to pay utilities to keep the spent fuel on site until a repository is built.
But according to Gawronski, states would be unlikely to accept any such plan.
"For the government to come out now and say, 'We'll pay you to keep it on site,' just wouldn't wash with the state commissioners," he said.

State regulators are also concerned that if utilities are required to keep the spent fuel on site, the storage costs will hit them and ratepayers at a time when they are struggling to compete in a deregulated power market.
"If they can't get rid of this stuff on site, it's going to be all the more difficult (to compete)," Gawronski said.
He gave Congress a 40 percent chance of passing a bill to build an interim storage site with enough votes to override a White House veto.
